messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Vega had spent most of her adult life running a large seaside hotel, a role that suited her precision and confidence, until the night that altered the texture of everything that came after. At 70, widowed and living alone now that her husband had died three years earlier, she still described herself as someone who used to handle pressure well. That certainty began to unravel after a police encounter outside her building, when officers, called to a disturbance, misread her attempt to explain what was happening and forced her against the hood of a car. She remembered the cold metal, the rough pressure at her wrists, the flashlight beam in her eyes, and the humiliating moment when her protests were ignored. What stayed with her most was not only the fear of being hurt, but the feeling that the very people who were supposed to protect her had turned on her. In the weeks that followed, she found herself replaying the scene in unwanted fragments while at work, especially when the lobby filled at check-in and a surge of guests pressed through the entrance. Crowded places became difficult to tolerate; a sudden jostle near the front desk or the sight of uniformed staff in the hotel corridor could make her heart leap and bring the whole event back with startling force. She had come to dread the anniversary of the incident as well, because even before the date arrived her body seemed to know it was approaching.

Marisol described her memory of that night as unusually sharp, almost photographic. She could call up the pattern of the officers’ badges, the smell of rain on asphalt, and the sound of her own voice becoming smaller as they spoke over her. In those moments of recall, she did not merely remember being afraid; the same terror returned with it, immediate and bodily, as if the event were happening again. That vividness made the memories harder to set aside, and the more clearly she saw them, the more convinced she became that she had been permanently changed. She said she did not know herself anymore, and that the woman who once managed a full hotel floor with ease and patience now seemed distant from the person who flinched at a crowded elevator or hesitated when a guest raised a hand too quickly. Her belief that the institutions meant to keep her safe had failed her deepened that sense of loss. She was certain that if the police could do this to her, then the world she had trusted as orderly and governed by rules was not what she had thought it was. That conviction did not stay abstract; it settled into the way she interpreted her own reactions, as proof that something essential in her had been damaged for good.

As the months passed, the same moments that stirred her distress also helped bind it tighter. The unwanted thoughts arrived most forcefully on busy days at the hotel, when too many people crossed the lobby at once, and they were especially punishing as the anniversary neared. Each return of the memory seemed to confirm her fear that she had changed permanently, and that the loss was not temporary but part of who she had become. In turn, that belief made the memory feel even more threatening: when it broke through without warning, in the middle of ordinary surroundings, it carried the force of evidence that she could no longer trust her own mind or her own life. Marisol began to limit her time near the front entrance, delegated more guest-facing tasks to younger staff, and avoided the busiest hours when she could. She told herself this was practical, but it also meant she spent more time watching from the edges of the lobby, scanning for anything that might set off another wave of terror. The more she watched for it, the more easily crowding, noise, or the sight of a uniform seemed to catch her off guard. By the time she finally sought help, she was exhausted by the cycle and frightened that the anniversary would bring another surge of memories she could not control. What she most wanted was to feel like herself again, but what frightened her most was the suspicion that the woman she had been was already gone.
